label: Institution
name: Australia and New Zealand Banking Group
summary:
Australia and New Zealand Banking Group (ANZ), one of the 'Big Four' Australian banks, traces its origins to the Bank of Australasia (1835) — founded in London to finance Australian colonial settlement — and is now (with AUD 1 trillion+ in assets) one of the Southern Hemisphere's largest banks, with particular strength in Asian banking (among the most Asia-focused of the major Australian banks) and Pacific island markets. ANZ's 2023 acquisition of Suncorp Bank created Australia's most significant banking consolidation in decades.

The Bank of Australasia (1835) — founded in London by investors supporting British colonial settlement — was one of the first banks established to serve the Australian colonies, financing wool and grain exports, pastoral loans, and colonial infrastructure. The Bank of New Zealand (1861) was founded separately; both were merged through ANZ's predecessor structures over the 20th century. ANZ in its current form emerged from the 1970 merger of the Australia and New Zealand Bank with the English, Scottish and Australian Bank.

ANZ's Asian strategy: under CEO Mike Smith (2007-2016), ANZ made a strategic push to become Australia's most internationally connected bank with a particular focus on Asia — acquiring stakes in Asian banks (AmBank Malaysia, PT Panin Bank Indonesia), growing Asian institutional business, and positioning itself as the primary banker for Australia-Asia trade flows. The 2023 AUD 4.9 billion Suncorp Bank acquisition — pending regulatory approval — would make ANZ the second-largest Australian bank by retail deposits.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: ANZ — descending from a London-founded colonial bank that financed Australian settlement, grown into a trillion-dollar institution, and now pursuing Asia's banking opportunities — traces the entire arc of Australian economic development from British colonial wool exports to 21st-century Indo-Pacific trade finance.
